What would happen to the Earth's atmosphere if all the insects disappeared
a: If all insects disappeared, Earth's atmosphere and ecosystems would undergo catastrophic changes that would ultimately make the planet uninhabitable for most life, including humans. Insects play critical roles in pollination — about 75% of global food crops depend on insect pollination, and without insects, agricultural production would collapse, leading to widespread famine and the breakdown of human civilization. The food web would collapse as well — insects are a primary food source for birds, bats, reptiles, amphibians, and fish, and the loss of these species would cascade through ecosystems. Without insects to decompose organic matter, dead plants and animals would accumulate, and the carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus cycles would be disrupted. The decomposition process, which insects accelerate by breaking down complex organic compounds, would slow dramatically, leading to the buildup of dead organic material and the release of greenhouse gases from incomplete decomposition. Soil health would deteriorate as insects like earthworms, ants, and beetles aerate the soil and cycle nutrients. Without these soil organisms, plant growth would decline, further exacerbating the collapse of ecosystems. The atmosphere would be affected indirectly — the massive die-off of plants and trees due to lack of pollination and soil degradation would reduce oxygen production and increase carbon dioxide levels, contributing to climate change. The loss of vegetation would also disrupt the water cycle, as plants play a crucial role in transpiration and precipitation patterns. Within a few years, most flowering plants would go extinct, followed by the animals that depend on them. The oceans would also be affected, as many marine species depend on insects and insect-like crustaceans in their food webs. The extinction of insects would represent one of the largest mass extinctions in Earth's history, fundamentally altering the composition and function of virtually every ecosystem on the planet. The atmospheric composition would gradually shift as plant die-offs reduce oxygen levels and increase carbon dioxide and methane concentrations, creating a feedback loop of environmental degradation.
